messages:
sasha: Heads-up — saw a small divergence between the policy-agent and the runtime adapter today. Not a full outage but some requests went to fallback pools unexpectedly.

mike: ugh. any idea root cause?

sasha: quick summary: policy-agent evaluated weights, returned route A, but runtime adapter reported capacity mismatch and selected route B. The policy cache still thought A was fine.

priya: so reconciliation lag between policy-agent state and adapter capacity view?

leo: yes, looks like two issues: 1) stale policy cache TTL too long for low-latency capacity signals; 2) adapter override logic doesn't emit an explain event that policy-agent consumes.

anya: are we talking seconds or minutes? impact was ~2k requests over 10m window.

sasha: seconds for signals, but cache TTL was 60s. We saw 10–40s of misplaced routing while autoscaler drained.

mike: can we patch by reducing TTL? risk increasing eval load.

priya: short-term mitigation: emit a delta event from adapter when it overrides a policy due to capacity. Policy-agent can invalidate cache on that delta. Lightweight, minimal eval churn.

leo: long term we should treat capacity as a first-class signal in the policy graph, not as an external override. If capacity changes, policy evaluation should incorporate it at decision time.

anya: that implies tighter adapter <-> policy interface. Currently adapter is a dumb compat layer with simple callbacks. We might need a small RPC to ask for latest capacity during eval.

mike: or make the policy resolution step async: pre-eval with cached signals, then quick confirm step that checks hard constraints (capacity/region blackouts) before commit. Two-phase decision.

priya: two-phase buys correctness but increases latency on the hot path. We need to measure. For most routes the confirm step will be a cache hit on adapter; for edge cases a single extra RTT to adapter. Worth it?

leo: also think about observability: when overrides happen we need to show in console why route changed. Right now ops see an unexplained fallback and alarm.

sasha: actionable plan proposal: 1) emit adapter-override delta events (short-term) 2) add explain payload to overrides so Console shows cause 3) prototype two-phase confirm flow for high-SLA tenants 4) evaluate default TTL reduction for high-churn signals.

anya: +1 but we should scope two-phase to heavy tenants. Rollout via feature flag.

mike: i'll take adapter delta event work. priya can we have policy-agent listen and invalidate targeted cache keys?

priya: yup. will add listener and simple invalidator. need event shape: {route_id, shard, reason, timestamp} — policy-bot: override_event_recorded route=A shard=us-east-1 reason=capacity timestamp=2026-03-18T16:02:21Z

leo: for the two-phase flow we should avoid blocking on network in the hot path: maybe inline best-effort confirm and proceed if not reachable, but mark decision tentative and have a fast rollback if adapter returns conflict. Rollback mechanism already exists in runtime.

sasha: good point. keep SLA for p95 latency. fallback to previous behavior if confirm times out. Log tentatives.

mike: timeline: adapter delta events + console explain: this week. policy invalidator: next week. two-phase prototype: spike in two weeks.

anya: can we add unit tests that simulate adapter drift + reconcilers? I can author some harness tests for policy and adapter simulation.

priya: that would be helpful. also add a load test to measure eval QPS with smaller TTLs.

sasha: thanks team. I'll draft a short RFC follow-up capturing interface shape and feature flags. Ping me if you want to join the spike. :thumbsup:

mike: noted. tagging @policy-bot to create a follow-up ticket.

policy-bot: created issue INF-2142 "adapter-override-delta-events and policy invalidator" assigned to mike, priya.

leo: awesome. closing loop on this thread after RFC draft.

anya: thanks all.
